question_text: According to the course material, delinquency can be viewed from four different perspectives: a parental view, an educational view, a mental health view, and a:
explanation: The course material identifies four perspectives on delinquency: a parental view (disruptive behaviour at home), an educational view (classroom disruption), a mental health view (a wide range of disruptive behaviours), and a legal system view (persons under 18 considered juvenile).

question_text: According to the course material, delinquent behaviour is divided into two categories: "status" offences, which would not be considered an offence if committed by an adult, and:
option_a: "Delinquency" offences, which involve destruction or theft of property and violent crimes
option_b: "Civil" offences, applicable only to disputes between adults
option_c: "Religious" offences, applicable only within places of worship
option_d: "International" offences, applicable only across national borders
explanation: Delinquent behaviour is divided into status offences (e.g. truancy, alcohol possession, curfew violations, which would not be offences if committed by an adult) and delinquency offences (property destruction/theft, violent crimes, illegal weapon possession).

question_text: According to Patterson (1986), cited in the course material, research showed that what percentage of antisocial behaviour in children was found to be the result of family interaction?
option_d: 0 percent; family interaction has no bearing on antisocial behaviour
explanation: Patterson's (1986) research discovered that 30 to 40 percent of antisocial behaviour was a result of family interaction, with a breakdown in parenting practices producing antisocial behaviour in children.

question_text: According to the course material, the oldest known set of written law against delinquency is the Code of Hammurabi, which listed a punishment specifically aimed at juveniles who disobeyed their parents, prescribing that if a son strikes his father, his:
option_b: Property shall be doubled in value
explanation: The Code of Hammurabi, the oldest known written law against delinquency, prescribed that if a son strikes his father, his hands shall be cut off, among other punishments aimed at juveniles who disobeyed their parents.

question_text: According to the course material, the legal codes of the New England colonies in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries reflected the Biblical Scripture of Deuteronomy 21:18-21, which prescribed that a stubborn and rebellious son who would not obey his father or mother should be brought before the elders and:
option_b: Given a formal written apology from his parents
option_c: Exempted from all future familial obligations
option_d: Sent to a foreign land for educational purposes
explanation: The New England colonial legal codes reflected Deuteronomy 21:18-21, prescribing that a stubborn and rebellious son who would not obey his parents should be brought before the elders of the city and stoned to death by all the men of the city.

question_text: According to Morris (1996), cited in the course material, adolescence is described as a buffer stage between childhood and adulthood, corresponding roughly to the teenage years and associated with:
option_b: Complete emotional stability with no conflict whatsoever
option_c: A period entirely free of any biological change
option_d: A stage occurring only in certain cultures, not universally
explanation: Morris (1996) describes adolescence as a buffer stage between childhood and adulthood, corresponding roughly to the teenage years, associated with emotional and social turmoil and a period of storm and stress.

question_text: According to the course material, the Alarmist view on peer groups holds that the period of adolescence and intense peer group activity is a time in a youth's life most likely to lead to conflict with adults, conventional institutions, and:
explanation: The Alarmists believe that the period of adolescence and intense peer group activity is most likely to lead to conflict with adults, conventional institutions, and the law, viewing rebellious group behaviour as an indication of extensive rejection of conventional values.

question_text: According to Herman and Julia Schwendinger, cited in the course material, delinquency is largely concentrated in social groups or networks independent of social class lines; the first such peer-status group, called the "socialites" or elites, is characterized by:
option_a: Imitating the lifestyles of the more affluent
option_b: Complete rejection of any lifestyle associated with wealth
option_c: Exclusive membership limited to only one gender
option_d: A total absence of any distinctive dress or language
explanation: According to Herman and Julia Schwendinger, the first peer-status group, called the "socialites" (also referred to as "gods", elites, or swingers), imitates the lifestyles of the more affluent.

question_text: According to Cesar F. Rebellon, cited in Reid (2006) in the course material's discussion of family and delinquency, research shows that many children from broken homes do not become delinquent, but that separation and divorce of parents are more strongly associated with delinquency than are:
option_b: Two-parent households with no history of separation
option_d: Households with more than three children
explanation: Rebellon, cited in Reid (2006), maintained that separation and divorce of parents are more strongly associated with delinquency than are single-parent households, challenging the simple assumption that broken homes alone cause delinquency.

question_text: According to the course material, the family court, otherwise known as the juvenile court because of its paternalistic philosophy, was first established in the United States in 1910, when it was known as the:
explanation: The family courts were first established in the United States in 1910, when they were called domestic relations courts, dealing with laws related to family matters including marriage, divorce, and juvenile adjudication.

question_text: According to the course material, the "Parens Patriae" doctrine, meaning "state as father", establishes that the state, rather than the parents, assumes:
option_b: No responsibility whatsoever for the welfare of children
option_c: Guardianship only over children with no living parents
option_d: Guardianship exclusively over children above the age of 18
explanation: The Parens Patriae doctrine states that the state, not the parent(s), assumes exclusive guardianship of children, acting as a benevolent parent responsible for the care and development of its children.

question_text: According to the course material, the 1962 Family Court Act of New York avoided the negatively-labeled term "juvenile delinquent" for children between 7 and 16 who were habitually truant, disobedient, or beyond parental control, instead using the label:
explanation: The 1962 Family Court Act of New York avoided the term "juvenile delinquent" and instead used the label "persons in need of supervision" (PINS) for children between 7 and 16 who were habitually truant, disobedient, or incorrigible.

question_text: According to the course material, the modern practice of legally separating adult and juvenile offenders can be traced to two developments in English custom and law: chancery courts and the:
explanation: The modern practice of separating adult and juvenile offenders traces to two English developments: the Poor Laws (a 1535 statute for placing neglected children with families for training) and chancery courts (protecting the property and welfare of affluent minors).

question_text: According to the course material, drugs frequently abused by youth are grouped into four classes: stimulants, narcotics, depressants, and:
explanation: The course material groups frequently abused drugs into four classes: stimulants (e.g. cocaine, amphetamine), narcotics (e.g. heroin, opium), depressants (e.g. barbiturates, alcohol), and cannabis.

question_text: According to the course material, on Nigerian streets, cocaine, a stimulant drug, is commonly referred to by the street name(s):
explanation: The course material notes that on Nigerian streets, cocaine (a stimulant) is called "snow" or "blow", while heroin (a narcotic) is called "gbana", "staff", or "horse", and cannabis is called "grass", "wee-wee", or "kaya".

question_text: According to Richard Cloward and Lloyd Ohlin (1960), cited in the course material, delinquency is the result of the great disparity between what youths are taught to have and what is actually available to them, such that youths who join a delinquent subculture want to achieve success but, since their legitimate path is blocked, turn to:
option_a: Illegitimate means in the form of delinquency
option_b: Immediate and complete abandonment of all personal goals
option_c: Formal legal channels exclusively, with no exception
option_d: A permanent renunciation of any further social interaction
explanation: Cloward and Ohlin (1960) argued that delinquency results from the disparity between what youths are taught to have and what is available to them; when the legitimate path is blocked, youths turn to illegitimate means to achieve success.
